intro: Fronting means putting at the start of a sentence an element that normally comes after the verb: “This I can't accept”, “Tired as she was, she kept going”, “Gone are the days when…”. It is used to link ideas, create contrast or express concession elegantly.
objectifs: Front an object or an adjective to create contrast (This I know; Lucky we were).
Build concessive clauses with fronting: Tired as I was…, Much as I like…, Try as she might…, Strange though it may seem…
Front adverbials and participles for cohesion and style (Of the 300 respondents…; Gone are the days…).
Distinguish fronting without inversion (This I know) from inversion after a negative element (Never have I…).

sections.titre: The principle: moving to link or contrast
texte: Normal English word order is subject + verb + complement. Fronting moves an element to the front for two main reasons: 1) to link the sentence to what came before (known information first), 2) to create a contrast with another idea.

In most cases, subject and verb stay in normal order after the fronted element: “This I can't accept” (not “This can't I accept”). Inversion only appears with certain elements: negatives (lesson 229), and participles or places followed by a noun subject (“Gone are the days”).
exemples: Most of the report is fine. This last paragraph, however, I can't accept.
Fronted object: contrast with the rest of the report.
She promised to finish by Friday, and finish she did.
Fronted verb: emphatic confirmation (and she really did).

sections.titre: Fronting an object or an adjective
texte: Fronting the object is most common with this, that, these, those, or with a noun in contrast: “Some things I'll forgive; lies I won't.” It is mainly spoken or literary, and very expressive.
A complement adjective can also come first, with an exclamatory or commenting effect: “Lucky we were to escape.” (The concessive form, below, is more frequent.)

lignes: I can do the maths, but not the writing.
The maths I can do; the writing, not so much.

exemples: The first exam I passed easily. The second was a nightmare.
Fronted object to contrast two exams.

sections.titre: Concessive clauses: Tired as I was…
texte: This is the most useful pattern at C1. Structure: adjective / adverb / noun + as (or though) + subject + verb, then the main clause. The meaning is “although”: “Tired as I was, I kept working” = Although I was very tired, I kept working.

Fixed variants: “Much as I like / admire / respect…” (= although I really like…); “Try as I might…” (= however hard I tried); “Strange / Hard as it may seem…”; “Child though he was…” (noun without article, very formal).
Note: in British English, don't add “as” at the start (“As tired as I was” is common in American English but can be read as a comparison). Never add “but” in the main clause.

lignes: Although I was tired, I finished the report.
Tired as I was, I finished the report.
Although I like him a lot, I don't trust him.
Much as I like him, I don't trust him.
Although she tried hard, she couldn't open it.
Try as she might, she couldn't open it.
Although it may seem strange, it works.
Strange as it may seem, it works.
Although he was very rich, he lived simply.
Rich though he was, he lived simply.

exemples: Hard as it may be to believe, the village had no electricity until 2015.
= Although it may be hard to believe…
Try as I might, I couldn't remember her name.
= However hard I tried…; “might” in a past context.

texte: Putting a time, place or quantity phrase first is very common in writing to organise information: “In 2020, …”, “Of the 300 respondents, 40 % said…”, “Among the most affected were…”. It is a cohesion tool: you start from what is known and move to what is new.

With a participle or adjective first, followed by “be”, you invert when the subject is a noun: “Gone are the days when…”, “Attached is a copy of the invoice”, “Included in the price are breakfast and Wi-Fi”. These forms are common in formal emails and journalism.
exemples: Of the 1,200 candidates, only 85 were selected.
Quantity first: start from the known group.
Gone are the days when a degree guaranteed a job.
= That time is over; participle + be + subject.
Among the guests were two former ministers.

texte: General rule: an ordinary element first → normal order (This I know). A negative or restrictive element first → inversion with an auxiliary (Never have I…). A place, participle or adjective + be / a verb of position, with a noun subject → inversion of the verb (Gone are the days; On the hill stood a church).
Fronting is expressive: in academic writing, keep to fronted adverbials (In 2020…, Of these…) and concessives; in speech, “This I know” or “That I doubt” are natural.

lignes: Cold as it was, we swam.

formule: Known or contrasted element first + subject + verb (This I know) · Adj. / adv. + as / though + subject + verb, main clause (Tired as I was, …) · Participle + be + noun subject (Gone are the days…)
prononciation: The fronted element is strongly stressed and forms its own intonation group: “THIS | I can't accept.”
In concessives, use a rise or fall-rise on the first part, then a fall on the main clause: “Tired as I WAS, | I kept GOing.”
“as” is reduced to /əz/: “Much as I like him” /ˈmʌtʃ əz aɪ ˈlaɪk ɪm/.
“though” is /ðəʊ/: “Rich though he was”; the “gh” is silent.
“Gone are the days”: stress “gone” and “days”, reduce “are the” to /ə ðə/.
erreurs: This can't I accept.
This I can't accept.
A fronted object does not cause inversion.
Tired as I was, but I kept going.
Tired as I was, I kept going.
The concessive replaces although: no “but” afterwards.
Although tired as I was, I finished.
Tired as I was, I finished. / Although I was tired, I finished.
Don't combine although with the as-structure.
Gone the days are when we could smoke inside.
Gone are the days when we could smoke inside.
Participle + be + noun subject.
Try as I could, I didn't find it.
Try as I might, I couldn't find it.
Fixed form: “try as I might”.
Much as I like him, but I don't trust him.
Much as I like him, I don't trust him.
No “but” after a concessive.
Attached you will find is the invoice.
Attached is the invoice. / Please find attached the invoice.
Two formulas that must not be mixed.

dialogue.contexte: In Montreal, a team leader explains to a colleague why he rejects part of a draft contract.
lignes: So, what do you think of the supplier's draft?
Most of it is fine. The penalty clause, though, I simply can't accept.
Really? Strange as it may seem, their lawyers say it's standard.
Standard it may be, but it's not fair to us.
Fronted adjective: he concedes the point, then objects.
Much as I agree, we need this contract. Gone are the days when we could pick and choose.
True. Of the five suppliers we contacted, they're the only one with stock.
Then let's propose a cap on the penalties. That they might accept.
Fronted object: “that” refers to the cap.
Good idea. I'll draft the email now: “Attached is our counter-proposal regarding clause 7.”
Participle + be + subject in a formal email.

mots: Fronting moves an element to the start.
putting an element at the beginning of a sentence
“Much as I like him” expresses concession.
accepting a point while keeping your view
Much as I'd like to stay, I have to go.
Try as I might, I couldn't sleep.
Gone are the days of cheap flights.
Enclosed is a cheque for 50 dollars.
Among the winners was a 12-year-old girl.
a person who answers a survey
They sent a counter-proposal the next day.
a new offer made in reply to an offer

exercices.consigne: Say whether the sentence shows fronting without inversion or inversion.
items: That I doubt very much.
fronting without inversion
Never have I been so embarrassed.
inversion
Cold as it was, we went swimming.
fronting without inversion
Gone are the days of paper tickets.
inversion (participle + be + subject)

exercices.consigne: Rewrite with the “… as / though …” structure.
items: Although she was exhausted, she finished the race.
Exhausted as she was, she finished the race.
Although I like my job a lot, I need a change.
Much as I like my job, I need a change.
Although he tried hard, he couldn't convince them.
Try as he might, he couldn't convince them.
Although it may sound strange, I enjoy exams.
Strange as it may sound, I enjoy exams.
Although the flat was small, it was very bright.
Small as / though the flat was, it was very bright.

exercices.consigne: Rewrite with the words in brackets at the front.
items: I can't accept [this decision].
This decision I can't accept.
Only 85 [of the 1,200 candidates] were selected.
Of the 1,200 candidates, only 85 were selected.
Breakfast and parking are [included in the price].
Included in the price are breakfast and parking.
The days when we wrote letters [are gone].
Gone are the days when we wrote letters.
Tired as I was, but I went out.
Tired as I was, I went out.
This can't I believe.
This I can't believe.
Try as I could, the door wouldn't open.
Try as I might, the door wouldn't open.

exercices.consigne: Rewrite each sentence with a fronting structure.
items: Although we were very tired, we carried on.
Tired as we were, we carried on / kept going.
The time when petrol cost a dollar is over.
Gone are the days when petrol (AmE: gas) cost a dollar.
However hard I tried, I couldn't understand.
Try as I might, I couldn't understand.

exercices.consigne: Write 3–4 sentences about a change in your town or job. Use at least two different fronting structures.
items: Example answer

Gone are the days when everyone in Yaoundé paid cash at the market. Of the traders I know, almost all now accept mobile money. Convenient as it is, the system still worries older customers. That, I think, is the real challenge for the next few years.

a_retenir: Fronting = moving an element to the front to link (known first) or contrast; usually no inversion (This I know).
Elegant concessives: Tired as I was…, Much as I like…, Try as I might…, Strange as it may seem… — with no although and no but.
Fronted adverbials for cohesion (Of the 300 respondents…); participle + be + noun subject with inversion (Gone are the days…, Attached is…).
Negative element first → auxiliary inversion; any other element → normal order.
